articles.title: Abbott agrees to settle DOJ lawsuit over baby formula plant contamination
articles.summary: Abbott Laboratories will pay $385 million to settle allegation related to how it operated a manufacturing plant tied to contaminated powdered baby formula suspected of causing infant deaths. Contamination led to the nation’s largest formula facility being shuttered temporarily in 2022, triggering a recall of several infant formula brands, including Similac, exacerbating existing supply chain…
articles.body:
Abbott Laboratories will pay $385 million to settle allegation related to how it operated a manufacturing plant tied to contaminated powdered baby formula suspected of causing infant deaths.

Contamination led to the nation’s largest formula facility being shuttered temporarily in 2022, triggering a recall of several infant formula brands, including Similac, exacerbating existing supply chain difficulties and causing a nationwide shortage.

The products were purchased with government funds under the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) program administered by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which pays for more than fifty percent of all infant formula sold in the United States.

The settlement “makes clear the safety of our children is not negotiable,” acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said in a statement.

The Justice Department (DOJ) had been considering criminal charges against the company, The Wall Street Journal reported , until the Trump administration closed the investigation in favor of a civil penalty.

The civil complaint from the DOJ alleges that Abbott knowingly manufactured infant formula purchased with taxpayer dollars “in an environment that put the products at unacceptable risk of microorganism contamination and significantly impacted the products’ reliability, quality, and safety.”

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) launched an inspection of the plant amid complaints that four infants had been hospitalized with rare bacterial infections after consuming powdered formula that was made in the facility. Two infants died from the infections.

The inspection found unsanitary conditions and multiple strains of a bacteria that can be deadly to infants. The facility was shuttered in February 2022, and reopened in June of that year.

The Justice Department’s complaint detailed those unsanitary conditions, including installing umbrellas to deal with roof leaks, which diverted water from production areas but created a wet environment ripe for bacterial growth.

Similarly, the complaint alleged that Abbott “intentionally did not test for bacterial growth to avoid obtaining positive test results showing contamination,” and that in certain instances where testing demonstrated micro contamination, Abbott failed to disclose the test results when responding to requests from FDA during 2019 and 2022 inspections.

Under the settlement, Abbott didn’t admit liability or fault. The company in a statement maintained there is no evidence that its formula caused the illnesses or deaths that prompted the 2022 recall.

The company said testing and genetic sequencing did not identify a connection between Abbott formula and the reported illnesses, which were caused by the bacterium Cronobacter sakazakii. The company also said that no unopened, distributed Abbott infant formulas have ever tested positive for Cronobacter sakazakii.

Nearly $349 million of the Abbott settlement funds will go to the federal government and just over $36 million will go to state Medicaid and WIC programs that purchased Abbott’s formula.

Three whistleblowers who first filed complaints about the plant will receive $69 million.

articles.title: Bessent says Treasury is seeking ways to deliver Trump's $5,000 dividend without adding to deficit
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told lawmakers on Tuesday that the US Treasury is examining whether the Trump administration can give Americans a $5,000 div...
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told lawmakers on Tuesday that the US Treasury is examining whether the Trump administration can give Americans a $5,000 dividend without going through Congress, and he believes there is a way to do it without adding to the deficit.

Testifying before the House Financial Services Committee, Bessent said Treasury officials have been developing the proposal for some time, though he declined to provide specifics on how the plan would be funded without driving up the nation's debt.

"That is in process right now," Bessent said. "I'm not ready to discuss it at present, but at Treasury, we've been working on it for quite a while."

"I think putting more money in the American people's pocket should be an objective for everyone, and I believe there are ways to do it that would not affect the deficit," he added.

If executive action isn't legally viable, Bessent said, the administration is prepared to take the legislative route. "If it becomes clear that we need congressional authority, I will meet with [House Speaker Mike Johnson], and I look forward to it."

At a Republican gathering in Dallas last week, President Trump promised to give every American a $5,000 "Trump Dividend" if the Republican Party wins in the midterms and maintains control of both the House and the Senate.

Analysts have estimated that sending a $5,000 check to every adult would cost 1.3 trillion.

articles.title: Dem rep asks Bessent to ‘talk sense’ into Trump on regulating AI
articles.summary: Democratic Rep. Stephen Lynch (Mass.) on Tuesday urged Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to convince President Trump to reverse course on regulating artificial intelligence (AI). During Bessent’s appearance before the House Financial Services Committee, Lynch said Trump does not have “a grasp” of “what we’re dealing with” regarding AI. “I’ll be honest, I don’t think the…
articles.body:
Democratic Rep. Stephen Lynch (Mass.) on Tuesday urged Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to convince President Trump to reverse course on regulating artificial intelligence (AI).

During Bessent’s appearance before the House Financial Services Committee, Lynch said Trump does not have “a grasp” of “what we’re dealing with” regarding AI .

“I’ll be honest, I don’t think the president could spell AI if I gave him the first letter,” quipped the Massachusetts Democrat, the ranking member of a House Financial Services subcommittee focused on AI.

The Commerce Department has worked with leading AI labs on evaluating models before they are deployed, under a voluntary program.

Earlier this summer, the Trump administration briefly held up new models from OpenAI and Anthropic, before allowing the companies to release their GPT 5.6 and Fables and Mythos models, respectively.

Trump has dismissed the need for beefed-up regulations on AI, even as industry leaders argue for reigning in the pace of development . Trump said Monday the only “guardrails” AI needs is a “STRONG AND SMART” president.

The president wrote on Truth Social , “We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!” adding there is a “SICK conspiracy” in the U.S. against AI and data centers.

During Tuesday’s hearing, Lynch credited Bessent with “suggesting some things” on AI “that are thoughtful and … cautionary.” The veteran lawmaker later said “we’ve lost control” of AI, referencing OpenAI recently hacking the systems of Hugging Face, which Nvidia announced it will purchase earlier this month.

“Do you think the president understands that it probably doesn’t matter whether the good guys develop a superintelligence or the bad guys develop a superintelligence?” Lynch remarked. “If you don’t have control of that entity, and it has preferences and goals that are inimical to the existence humanity, it won’t matter.”

Bessent pushed back, saying it “matters a great deal” whether the U.S. or China lead on AI. Lynch then cut the Treasury secretary off, reiterating his view that “the entity itself is what is the danger to us all,” not the possibility of China leading on AI.

“We keep hearing about this race, this race against China. … Well, we don’t control the entity that we’re trying to create, and neither does China,” Lynch said.

“What I’m saying is, I hope there’s a way that you might be able to talk sense to the president about AI and the threat that you and I know it presents,” the Massachusetts lawmaker later told Bessent.

Bessent responded saying Trump was “completely aligned” with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on AI development. While Huang was speaking at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles on Monday, Trump called him and said concerns about AI were a “hoax.”

“The data centers are great, and they make people wealthy, and they make states wealthy,” the president said after Huang put him on speaker phone, according to a video summit attendee Ben Pouladian shared online .

Earlier this month, Huang urged policymakers to regulate “practical and actual” harms of AI instead of “theoretical and hypothetical” effects.

“We want to make sure that the technology advances in a safe way and … the more advanced it is, the safer and more practical it could be,” Huang told reporters at the G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, N.C.

articles.title: Bessent calls Treasury bond buyback successful, reiterates he has tools to stabilize bond market
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Tuesday said his intervention in the bond market last week was "successful," while reiterating that he has the tools to t...
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Tuesday said his intervention in the bond market last week was "successful," while reiterating that he has the tools to take further action.

Bessent was asked during a hearing before the House Financial Services Committee whether the Treasury's decision to buy back $6 billion in long-dated government bonds was successful, given that the yield on the 10-year Treasury bond has risen since then. Bessent encouraged looking at the "counterfactual" of what it would have done, suggesting the yield could have been even higher. He pointed out that the Treasury subsequently held two of the most successful bond auctions in 20 years.

On Sept. 10, Treasury sought to buy back up to $6 billion of government debt , triple the normal buyback operation and far above Bessent's Aug. 19 announcement that the department would at least double the amount of long-term bonds it buys back. The actions are aimed at keeping government debt markets liquid, but the measures have been viewed as an effort to put a lid on Treasury yields.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury breached 5% Tuesday, a level not seen since 2007, as oil prices have marched higher on renewed tensions in the Middle East, inflation concerns , and soaring US debt. The US national debt recently crossed $40 trillion .

When asked whether the US needs to tackle its debt problem to bring down yields, Bessent concurred but said it's just one of the forces driving up the 10-year yield.

Bessent also again promised a "fiscal consolidation" plan coming soon, without offering any details.

As Treasury finishes drafting rules for the GENIUS Act, the 2025 law governing stablecoins, Bessent predicted an increase in demand for US safe-haven assets, especially Treasury bills. The implication is that it could push down bond yields, while simultaneously buttressing the dollar against other currencies.

articles.title: Crypto bill falls short in early hurdle on Senate floor
articles.summary: A cryptocurrency regulation bill failed to advance on the Senate floor Tuesday, after all Democrats and a few Republicans blocked a procedural vote. The Senate voted 49-50 on a motion to proceed with consideration of the Clarity Act, failing to reach the required 60-vote threshold. It marks a major setback for the industry, which has long pushed for the measure setting up a regulatory…
articles.body:
A cryptocurrency regulation bill failed to advance on the Senate floor Tuesday, after all Democrats and a few Republicans blocked a procedural vote .

The Senate voted 49-50 on a motion to proceed with consideration of the Clarity Act, failing to reach the required 60-vote threshold. It marks a major setback for the industry, which has long pushed for the measure setting up a regulatory framework for the crypto market.

Four Republicans — Sens. Susan Collins (Maine), Josh Hawley (Mo.), Jerry Moran (Kan.) and Thom Tillis (N.C.) — split with the rest of their party to oppose the measure.

The vote Tuesday came amid a flurry of last-minute efforts to strike a deal between Republicans and crypto-friendly Democrats.

About a dozen Democrats were considered potential yes votes. But they ultimately declined to support the legislation after the two sides failed to reach an agreement on ethics rules amid lingering concerns about President Trump and his family’s involvement in the crypto industry.

Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.) slammed her Democratic colleagues Tuesday, suggesting the vote “proved they were never truly serious about protecting consumers and preserving American leadership.”

“I sat at the table with Senate Democrats working in good faith to get this done while they played games,” she said in a statement. “For over a year, they presented demands and the second we met them, they made new demands and moved the goal posts.”

Senate Republicans put forward what an aide described as their “last, best and final offer” on Sunday, unveiling updated bill text with changes to the ethics language and a several other sections at the heart of negotiations.

The new White House-approved ethics provision builds on earlier language that barred public officials, including the president, from issuing or sponsoring crypto assets.

It initially only gave enforcement power to the Department of Justice (DOJ). But after pushback from Democrats, the latest version also allows state attorneys general to bring cases against the agency or crypto exchanges over violations.

This still fell short for Democrats. Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) suggested Monday that there were “a whole lot of loopholes” in the new ethics language.

“I will tell you this: Democrats should not advance a bill that does not address the Trump family’s approach to this, where they’re clearly focused on enriching themselves,” he told reporters.

Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), who has been a central player in negotiations, accused GOP leadership Tuesday of ending talks and forcing a vote “just as Democrats and Republicans were making progress to address ethics concerns.”

“This legislation failed squarely because Republicans refuse to say no to the president,” he added in a statement. “It takes 60 votes to pass a bill, and instead of spending their time twisting themselves into knots to appease President Trump, Republicans should have worked more closely with Senate Democrats to craft a bill that could pass with strong ethics provisions.”

articles.title: Texas’s Arch Manning apologizes for laughing at AI video of coach slapping female reporter
articles.summary: Texas quarterback Arch Manning issued an apology Tuesday after he laughed during a press conference this week about an AI-generated video depicting his coach, Steve Sarkisian slapping ESPN reporter Holly Rowe. Referencing the press conference on Monday, Manning said he made an “insensitive comment about an AI video.” “There is nothing funny about it,” he…
articles.body:
Texas quarterback Arch Manning issued an apology Tuesday after he laughed during a press conference this week about an AI-generated video depicting his coach, Steve Sarkisian slapping ESPN reporter Holly Rowe.

Referencing the press conference on Monday, Manning said he made an “insensitive comment about an AI video.”

“There is nothing funny about it,” he said. “It’s easy to say I didn’t mean it, but I know my words and actions were hurtful to a lot of people. I do not take that lightly and am deeply sorry for that.”

Manning, a day earlier, had been asked if he had seen viral social media content surrounding the Longhorns win over Ohio State, specifically a decision by Sarkisian to blow off a postgame interview with Rowe, one of ESPN’s top reporters.

“Did you see that one,” Manning asked reporters in the room while laughing. “Of him slapping Holly Rowe.”

The video in question was an AI-generated clip that showed the Texas coach slapping Rowe and yelling “Hook Em!” before running off.

“I specifically want to apologize to [Rowe] because of what she has had to deal with because of my comments. I have a ton of respect for her and appreciate her showing me grace in this moment,” he continued. “I need to do better and will be more thoughtful going forward.”

Manning is the nephew of Hall of Fame NFL quarterback’s Eli and Peyton Manning and the grandson of legendary signal caller Archie Manning.

He is considered one of the best quarterbacks in the country and is on the short list of Heisman candidates this season, likely to be taken highly in next spring’s NFL draft.

With their fourth quarter comeback win over Ohio State on Saturday, The Longhorns jumped to the No. 1 spot in the AP Top 25 poll.

articles.body: Most of us hand over a lot of personal information to the DMV because we have no choice. Your address, birth date, driver's license information and other identifying details can all end up in government systems. That is why a breach involving driver records deserves attention. Florida officials have now confirmed that the Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles, or FLHSMV, experienced a data breach. The agency says it learned about the incident on Sept. 4, quickly mitigated it and has seen no further breach or ongoing unauthorized access. The confirmation follows claims from the ShinyHunters extortion group that it accessed Florida's Driver and Vehicle Information Database, known as DAVID, and stole more than 200,000 driver records. Florida has not confirmed that record count or publicly said exactly what information was taken. You’ll learn how to organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare questions for your next doctor’s visit. No technical experience is needed. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com Florida confirms the DMV data breach FLHSMV says its investigation traced the breach to credentials belonging to a single Plant City Police Department user. According to the agency, those credentials were improperly stored on the employee's personal electronic device. A criminal actor was then able to take advantage of them. That explanation gives us the first official account of how the breach occurred. It also differs from the access method ShinyHunters previously described. FLHSMV says it notified the Florida Office of the Attorney General as required under state law. The agency is also working with the Florida Digital Service and Florida Department of Law Enforcement. The criminal investigation remains ongoing. Officials say additional information will be released at an appropriate time. What ShinyHunters claims it stole from Florida ShinyHunters says it stole more than 200,000 driver records from DAVID. BleepingComputer reported that the group provided a screenshot of a DAVID record belonging to Jeffrey Epstein as evidence that it had accessed the system. The screenshot reportedly contained an address, Social Security number, birth date, driver's license information and registered vehicle details. DAVID can contain far more than a person's basic driver's license information. Government records describing the system show that authorized users may have access to driver information, photographs, signatures, vehicle history, insurance information and other identifying records. However, FLHSMV still has not disclosed how many records were accessed or stolen. The agency also has not confirmed ShinyHunters' claim that more than 200,000 records were taken. CyberGuy reached out to FLHSMV for additional comment, but did not hear back before our deadline. Florida's findings conflict with the hackers' password-reset claim ShinyHunters originally told BleepingComputer that it breached DAVID through a password-reset flaw. The group claimed that weakness allowed it to compromise multiple accounts, allegedly including accounts belonging to DMV employees and an FBI agent. ShinyHunters said it then moved through DAVID record IDs and downloaded associated pages and driver files beginning Sept. 3. The group later said it had lost access and believed the password-reset issue was being patched. Florida's investigation now points somewhere else. FLHSMV says the attacker took advantage of credentials belonging to one Plant City Police Department user that had been improperly stored on a personal electronic device. The agency has not backed ShinyHunters' claim that a password-reset flaw allowed the group to compromise multiple accounts. So, for now, the password-reset explanation remains ShinyHunters' version of events, while compromised police credentials are the access method Florida has publicly identified. Why Florida's DAVID database holds sensitive information DAVID serves authorized government users rather than ordinary public searches. FLHSMV says its Bureau of Records manages access to driver records through DAVID for law enforcement and other approved entities. The agency also audits users for compliance. Florida policy treats personal information in motor vehicle records as confidential. That information can include Social Security numbers, driver identification numbers, addresses and medical or disability information. That kind of information can give criminals powerful material for identity theft. Imagine getting a call from someone claiming to represent a government agency. The caller already knows your address, birth date and driver's license information. Suddenly, the scam sounds far more convincing. IS YOUR SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER ON THE DARK WEB? ShinyHunters claims other state DMV systems are being targeted BleepingComputer previously reported that a source said the attackers were targeting DMV platforms in other states through social engineering. ShinyHunters also told the outlet it expected additional DMV breaches to surface. There has been no confirmation from Florida that the current breach involved other state DMV systems. Still, the possibility deserves attention because state motor vehicle agencies hold information that can be extremely valuable for identity fraud and targeted scams. If criminals find a technique that works against one government system, they often look for similar access elsewhere. Who is ShinyHunters? ShinyHunters is an extortion operation associated with data theft attacks against companies and online services. Threat actors using the name have been linked to attacks involving Salesforce environments and companies including Google, Cisco and Match Group. More recently, the attackers have used voice phishing, also called vishing. In these attacks, someone impersonates IT support and tries to convince an employee to enter credentials or authentication codes into a phishing site. The attackers have also targeted single sign-on accounts connected to services such as Microsoft 365, Google Workspace and Salesforce. FLHSMV referred to the attacker in its statement only as an "international cybercriminal organization." The agency did not publicly identify ShinyHunters by name. So, while ShinyHunters has claimed responsibility and Florida has confirmed a breach, Florida has not publicly attributed the attack to the group. Still, this shows why protecting trusted accounts has become so important. Once an attacker gets legitimate credentials, other connected services may become accessible too. 8 ways to stay safe if your DMV data may be exposed You do not need to wait for a confirmed case of identity theft before protecting yourself. These steps can make stolen personal information harder for criminals to use. 1) Freeze your credit A credit freeze can make it harder for someone to open new credit accounts in your name. You need to place a freeze separately with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Credit freezes are free. You can temporarily lift one when you legitimately need a lender to access your credit. 2) Review your credit reports Check your credit reports for new accounts or inquiries you do not recognize. You can request your reports through AnnualCreditReport.com, the federally authorized source for free credit reports. Also keep an eye on your financial accounts. Small unfamiliar transactions can sometimes be an early warning sign. 3) Be suspicious of Florida DMV messages A confirmed breach creates a ready-made lure for scammers. You could receive a text, email or phone call claiming your Florida driver information was exposed. Be especially careful if the sender pressures you to verify personal information or click a link. Instead, visit FLHSMV through its official website at flhsmv.gov/ yourself. Keep your antivirus software running and updated on your computers and mobile devices. Give it a strong, unique password and use a password manager to create and securely store it. Then turn on multifactor authentication. Whenever possible, consider an authenticator app or passkey rather than relying only on codes sent by text message. 6) Watch for identity theft Review bank accounts, credit cards and other important services for activity you do not recognize. Also pay attention to unexpected government correspondence. A strange tax notice or benefits letter could signal that someone has used your identity. Removing that data cannot erase records stolen during a breach. However, reducing the information available elsewhere can make it harder for criminals to build a detailed profile and create convincing scams. These services can also keep checking for information that reappears over time. FLHSMV has not yet publicly disclosed how many people were affected or exactly what information was taken. Do not automatically trust an email simply because it mentions DAVID or the Florida DMV. Avoid using links in unexpected messages. Go directly to the agency's official website to verify any notice. Kurt's key takeaways Florida has now confirmed the breach, but some of the biggest questions remain unanswered. ShinyHunters claims it stole more than 200,000 driver records, while Florida says the attacker got in using credentials belonging to a Plant City Police Department user that were improperly stored on a personal device. What we still do not know is exactly how much information was taken or whose records were exposed. Until Florida releases more details, I would take this seriously. articles.title: Iran war likely to drive up inflation next year, CBO says
articles.summary: The U.S. war against Iran is likely to drive up inflation early next year and could cost at least $2 billion a month as long as it continues, according to a new report from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO). The CBO estimated in its Tuesday report that the main economic impact of the conflict…
articles.body:
The U.S. war against Iran is likely to drive up inflation early next year and could cost at least $2 billion a month as long as it continues, according to a new report from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO).

The CBO estimated in its Tuesday report that the main economic impact of the conflict is made of pressures caused by the disruptions to shipping through the Red Sea and the reduction of natural gas and oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

The reduction in shipments has increased energy prices and because of it, in the first quarter of 2027, inflation is estimated to be 0.5 percentage points higher than what CBO projected in February this year.

“The agency estimates that the higher rates of inflation attributable to the conflict will boost interest rates on Treasury securities. In CBO’s assessment, interest rates on 3-month Treasury bills are nearly 0.2 percentage points higher in 2026 than the agency estimated this past February,” CBO said in the 19-page report. “By the first half of 2027, such rates are less than 0.1 percentage point higher than previously estimated.”

The war against Iran has cost the Pentagon around $38 billion as of Aug. 1 this year, CBO estimated when factoring in replacing expended munitions, flying hours, assets lost in the conflict and increased fuel costs.

The Pentagon told Congress on Aug. 13 that the cost of war has gone up to over $42 billion, The Hill reported on Tuesday.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told the Senate during a hearing in July that the estimated cost of the conflict was $37.5 billion.

“Trump’s illegal war with Iran is a one-two punch that’s burning a hole in Americans’ pockets and burning a hole in our munitions supply, hurting our military readiness,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), who sits on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said in a statement. “This war is a betrayal of the American people, and it needs to end.”

The main cost for the Pentagon would be the “large expenditure” of missile defense interceptors, leaving the U.S. with a reduced inventory for “several years,” according to CBO.

The CBO report came a day after a report from the Pentagon’s watchdog said that U.S. diplomatic facilities in four Gulf countries – Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) – suffered around $184 million in estimated damages from Iranian military strikes.

The watchdog said that the U.S. conflict with Iran “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply” regarding advanced weapons systems.

President Trump and Hegseth have repeatedly said that the U.S. has sufficient weapons stockpiles.

“CBO estimates that the cost to replace the munitions expended through August 1, 2026, is $21.7 billion: $7.3 billion for the land-attack cruise missiles, $13.1 billion for the missile defense interceptors, and $1.2 billion for other munitions,” CBO said in the report.

articles.title: What if social media isn’t hurting kids?
articles.summary: In a new book, Restoring Childhood, psychology researcher Peter Gray challenges social psychologist Jonathan Haidt’s popular theory about the 2010s decline in teen mental health.
articles.body: Two years ago, social psychologist Jonathan Haidt released his New York Times bestseller The Anxious Generation. The book posits that the rise of social media and smartphone use is largely to blame for the prominent decline in teen mental health since 2010. It quickly became a central rallying cry of the social media backlash. Haidt has been credited with helping inspire Australia’s nationwide teen social media ban. He has joined forces with bereaved parents who are fighting tech companies in court. His name comes up unprompted in conversations with people in power who say his book opened their eyes to an online crisis. Haidt’s theory has received regular critiques from recognized academics. Candice Odgers, a leading adolescent mental health researcher, wrote a scathing review of Haidt’s analysis in Nature that opened by conceding, “this book is going to sell a lot of copies, because Jonathan Haidt is telling a scary story about children’s development that many parents are primed to believe.” Now, in the wake of that highly accurate prediction, a former colleague of Haidt’s seeks to not only take down his theory, but also offer an alternative. The biggest question may not be whether he’s correct — but whether it’s too late to change course if he is. [Media: In his new book Restoring Childhood, psychology researcher Peter Gray argues that teens’ mental health declined thanks to decades of steadily reduced autonomy, and after a brief period of reprieve, fell again in the 2010s not — as Haidt argues — because of phones and social media, but because of rigid schooling methods linked to the Common Core curriculum and government pressure to improve children’s performance. And far from being damaging, Gray also argues the adoption of home internet in the 1990s and 2000s actually drove a rebound in teens’ mental health by restoring freedom and connection lost in earlier decades. He fears social media bans aren’t just — as Odgers has argued — a distraction from real solutions, but a new harm in themselves. In an interview on The Vergecast, Gray told me that Haidt’s book “completely ignored” dozens of meta-analyses and other research that’s found “not even a meaningful correlation between the amount of time kids are on social media or on smartphones and their mental health.” Where there is some connection, Gray adds, studies suggest that teens may use social media to cope with their depression or anxiety. He references a study in Florida that found 11-to-13-year-olds who owned smartphones were more likely to spend real-world time with friends. “You take a smartphone away from your kids and that study suggests you’ll make them less happy and they’ll have less friends,” he says. Gray says that in studies through the years, kids consistently identify school pressure, not social media, as their top source of anxiety. “That doesn’t mean it’s the primary source for everybody, but when you’re looking at the population at large, every single study that I’ve been able to find where kids are asked, ‘What’s the primary source of your anxiety or your stress or your depression?’, in every single one of them, school pressure comes out on top,” Gray tells me. “Nothing else comes close.” Gray and Haidt both believe that since at least the 1980s, increased restrictions on kids’ independence and unstructured play have damaged their resilience. While it used to be common for kids to play together unsupervised, that practice has diminished in part due to the rise of “stranger danger” narratives fostered by rare, but high-profile, crimes. In 2017 the pair helped cofound an organization called Let Grow, which advocates for policies that make it easier for parents to let their children play freely, like ensuring they can’t be considered neglectful for letting kids outside by themselves. But the two have split sharply over the impact of the internet. Gray’s book is intended as a deliberate rebuttal to Haidt’s — after The Anxious Generation’s release, Gray resigned from the board of Let Grow to avoid conflict within the organization. Haidt did not respond to a request for comment from The Verge, but he told The Atlantic’s Kaitlyn Tiffany in a July article that the 1990s and early 2000s dip in teen suicide rates may be credited to a phase-out of leaded gasoline, since lead exposure has been linked to mental health issues. He also told Tiffany that Gray relied too heavily on a minority dissenting group of researchers. Tiffany writes that many of the more than a dozen tech and child development researchers she spoke to “expressed concern that Haidt overstates the strength of correlational findings and suggests causation where it hasn’t been proved.” Gray accuses Haidt of stirring a moral panic over technology that isn’t, on the whole, harmful. Looking across research, he says, Common Core is the clearest explanation for the sudden decline in teen mental health. And at the population level, the impact of social media “balances out. Some kids are doing better, some kids are doing worse because they’re on social media.” Gray says he’s not opposed to all guardrails, including school phone bans and the concept of age verification for accessing pornography. But he questions the effectiveness of bans on social media, knowing kids are likely to get around them, and is hesitant to restrict platforms that let kids express themselves — suggesting instead that parents focus on teaching their children to navigate them. “We need to stop treating kids as if they’re idiots,” he told me. “We need to start understanding that kids are pretty good at knowing what’s good for them and not good for them and they can benefit from our help in learning how to do these things.” But increasingly, parents of younger teens may not have that choice. Haidt’s theory holds undisputed dominance in many circles, including among politicians. Since Australia’s social media ban for teens, the UK and European Union are among those considering their own bans or platform limits. In the US, states like California and New York have enacted limits on certain social media features, and a federal proposal would restrict algorithmic feeds for kids under 17. Even among people who find Gray’s arguments about Common Core convincing, some might still see taking kids offline as a harmless precaution. With so much momentum behind the backlash against phones and social media, can Gray’s book still make a difference? “I certainly hope it’s not too late,” he says. He points out that some moral panics have petered out. In the 1990s and 2000s, for instance, many people worried that video games like Mortal Kombat and Doom were making kids more violent, connecting their rise to that of school shootings. Eventually, research showed many mass shooters didn’t play video games after all. Attempts at regulation — including a California ban on the sale of violent games to children — were largely overruled. And many kids who did play them grew up to become those in charge. “The science won out eventually,” Gray says. “So it’s not me that’s going to win out. It’s the science that’s going to win out.”

articles.title: US-China Discuss Cutting Some Tariffs as Leaders Prepare to Meet
articles.summary: Prospects for an extension to the US-China trade truce are solidifying as the two sides discuss slashing tariffs on goods including American energy and agric...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Prospects for an extension to the US-China trade truce are solidifying as the two sides discuss slashing tariffs on goods including American energy and agricultural products ahead of the leaders' summit next week.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday he'll meet this weekend with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, ahead of the summit between President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping set for Sept. 24 in Washington.

Earlier, Bloomberg News reported the US and China are discussing lowering tariffs on certain goods. Next week's meetings are also likely to result in an agreement to cut duties on Chinese inputs for manufacturers, according to people familiar with the matter.

The moves are expected to be carried out under an earlier plan for reciprocal tariff cuts on roughly $30 billion in trade. Most-favored-nation rates would be applied to some items from China, said the people, who requested anonymity in order to discuss private conversations.

An extension of the one-year trade truce would remove one potential stumbling block for a world economy grappling with wars in Iran and Ukraine, elevated oil prices and rekindling inflation concerns that are pushing up global borrowing costs. Still, expectations for the summit remain tempered by China's relations with Iran and Russia as well as competition over leading-edge technologies such as artificial intelligence.

Bessent, speaking before the House Financial Services Committee, said he looked forward to speaking with the Chinese vice premier about sanctions related to the war in Iran as the US increases economic pressure on the Islamic Republic.

Echoing Trump, the Treasury secretary has consistently emphasized the importance of maintaining the US lead over China in AI, an area where Chinese firms have been gaining ground on their Silicon Valley rivals.

"It does matter whether the good guys or the bad guys have this," Bessent said. "As a person who manages the relationship with China on AI, it matters a great deal."

Competition over AI has emerged as a key source of friction.

Last week, three US national security agencies accused Chinese AI firms including DeepSeek and Moonshot AI — the maker of the breakthrough Kimi K3 model — of systematically extracting proprietary knowledge from American firms. While the Chinese companies have refrained from commenting on the US allegations, China's government has pushed back forcefully on the claims.

articles.title: Airport X-ray shows terrifying object taped in carry-on to skip checked baggage fee
articles.summary: A traveler at Dane County Regional Airport in Wisconsin taped a knife inside her carry-on bag to avoid paying a $100 baggage fee ahead of a camping trip, the TSA reported.
articles.body: A traveler tried to dodge a $100 baggage fee by hiding a dangerous item inside her carry-on bag — but it wasn't long before she was caught red-handed. The unidentified passenger was going through security at Dane County Regional Airport in Madison, Wisconsin, when a TSA officer spotted what appeared to be a knife on an X-ray machine, according to an employee story published on the agency's website. Officers searched the bag and discovered the knife had been taped in place inside the luggage, according to TSA. TSA OFFICER SEES ALARMING SHAPES ON X-RAY BEFORE STOLEN CIVIL WAR MYSTERY UNRAVELS The passenger later admitted she tried to conceal the knife from TSA because she had an upcoming camping trip, the agency said. "Her response to me was, 'I was attempting to conceal this knife from TSA,'" Supervisory TSA Officer Andrew Kasten said. The admission, along with the discovery of the concealed knife, prompted Kasten to call law enforcement. The Dane County Sheriff's Office and TSA Manager Annie Lu responded to the scene, TSA said. The woman told officers she did not think TSA would find the knife. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER She said she chose not to check her luggage because she wanted to avoid a $100 baggage fee, according to the agency. She did not think TSA would find the knife. TSA Officer Callie Meis, who has worked for the agency for 22 years, first flagged the bag for additional screening after spotting the suspected knife on the X-ray. "I have encountered many knives over the years, but never in this position within a bag," Kasten said. Jim Kohn, who has worked for TSA for 21 years, said he's encountered knives that accidentally slipped through holes in purses, bag liners or jacket pockets. In this case, however, the passenger acknowledged deliberately securing the knife with tape. "Our team does a great job making sure every possible threat is found when we need to conduct additional screening," Kohn said. "When contemplating the options of saving a few dollars or paying a federal civil penalty due to something hidden, I recommend being smart about it," Kasten said. "For whatever reason you may be traveling, don't jeopardize your income or freedom just to save an item like this $5 knife." articles.title: House passes Iran war powers resolution
articles.summary: The House on Tuesday passed a Democratic-backed war powers resolution that would limit President Trump’s military actions in Iran. The lower chamber voted 220-204 to pass the resolution, sponsored by Rep. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.). Seven Republicans voted in favor of the measure: Reps. Thomas Massie (Ky.), Brian Fitzpatrick (Pa.), Warren Davidson (Ohio), Tom Barrett (Mich.), Mariannette Miller-Meeks…
articles.body:
The House on Tuesday passed a Democratic-backed war powers resolution that would limit President Trump’s military actions in Iran.

The lower chamber voted 220-204 to pass the resolution, sponsored by Rep. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.). Seven Republicans voted in favor of the measure: Reps. Thomas Massie (Ky.), Brian Fitzpatrick (Pa.), Warren Davidson (Ohio), Tom Barrett (Mich.), Mariannette Miller-Meeks (Iowa), Zach Nunn (Iowa) and Nancy Mace (S.C.).

It was the third time the House has passed a similar war powers resolution, but the number of Republicans in support increased from four to seven.

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, argued in remarks on the House floor Tuesday that “this Congress has not authorized a war with Iran. And yet this administration has kept our troops in harm’s way, without a declaration of war, without an authorization from Congress and without any plan for how to win or end the war.”

“The administration hasn’t just continued to wage this illegal war in direct violation of the Constitution; it’s done so while Americans bear the costs: 19 fallen service members, and more than 750 service members wounded, extended troop deployments, and billions of dollars in additional spending. The president’s mismanagement of this war has hurt America’s ability to prepare for future threats,” Meeks added.

A report from the Pentagon’s watchdog made public on Monday found that U.S. diplomatic facilities in four Gulf countries suffered around $184 million in estimated damages from Iranian military strikes.

The disclosures about the damage to U.S. outposts come as the cost of the conflict has gone up since it began in late February.

The Pentagon told congressional defense committees last month that the cost of the war is at least $42 billion.

A new report from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office said that the conflict will likely spike inflation early next year and could cost at least $2 billion a month as long as the war continues.

In addition, 18 U.S. service members have been killed and more than 800 wounded in the more than six-month war. Over 50,000 American troops are still deployed to the region, with the Trump administration yet to provide a clear exit strategy from the deeply unpopular conflict.

Last week, Trump said he believes that the war against Iran would end “immediately” after November’s midterm elections.

Massie on Tuesday introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of launching an illegal war not approved by Congress.

articles.title: Petrol and diesel price rises push UK inflation higher
articles.summary: Summer holidays and disruption to global oil supplies by the Middle East conflict stoked price growth.
articles.body:
Rises in petrol, diesel and airfares pushed UK inflation up to its highest level in six months in the year to August.

Inflation accelerated to 3.1% from 2.9% , according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

The cost of filling up a vehicle soared in August as the conflict in the Middle East continued to disrupt global oil supplies. Petrol prices jumped to their highest for nearly four years, the ONS said, while diesel also rocketed.

Meanwhile, the cost of flying jumped during the key month for summer getaways.

Overall, motor fuel prices rose by 23% compared to August last year.

Oil hit more than $91 a barrel as the US-Israel war with Iran went on. That compares to around $73 just before hostilities began earlier this year.

As a result, average petrol prices have continued to climb and between July and August, they rose by 9.1p to 161.3p per litre.

"This is the highest price recorded since November 2022," said the ONS. At that point, Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine had pushed up global energy costs.

Capital Economics said, at this point, the effect of higher oil prices has not spilled over into other areas such as food and drink, where the pace of inflation remained at 1.3% in the year to August.

But its chief UK economist, Paul Dales, said: "Everyone knows that bigger rises in inflation are on their way."

Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS, said: "Rising crude oil and petrol prices increased both the annual cost of raw materials and the price of goods leaving factories respectively."

Dales estimates that a combination of higher oil and gas prices and "the eventual 'first-round' effect of businesses passing on some of their higher energy costs" will lead to inflation peaking at 4.2% in January.

As well as hitting drivers in the pocket, higher oil prices also affect forecourts.

Goran Raven, owner of Essex petrol station RJ Raven, told the BBC: "Things are down. We've got lots of pressure on us at the moment. I'd say we're about 20% down on this time last year."

Raven said changes in the oil price have a "real-time impact on us".

In recent days, Brent crude - the global benchmark for oil prices - has surpassed $100 a barrel.

"We only have small tanks here, so we need a tanker almost every day at the moment and we have to pay a daily spot price," said Raven. "When the price goes up, we have to go up with it. There's no way around it.

"The margins here are wafer-thin on fuel. People like to think we're earning a lot on it. Unfortunately, we really aren't. It's single digits of pence we earn per litre."

articles.title: EU Proposes Canada Become the Bloc’s First ‘Associate Member’
articles.summary: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union.

She offered the invitation during her state of the union address in Strasbourg, France, Wednesday, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in attendance.

"In this new world, we must urgently re-imagine our partnerships and build global coalitions for our resilience and democracies," von der Leyen said. "I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada being the first associate member of the European Union."

Carney warned earlier this year that the "rules-based international order" was effectively dead and has made repeated calls for so-called middle powers to band together to oppose the pressure tactics and intimidation of the world's dominant economies. Bloomberg reported earlier that the transatlantic allies were in talks to forge a new alliance to ensure their security.

Von der Leyen also discussed closer cooperation with Canada on manufacturing, tech, defense and energy, and cited the Arctic as a "flagship joint project."

Canada's priority list includes concluding the ratification of CETA, the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, an accord that was negotiated a decade ago but that still hasn't been formally approved by 10 European countries, according to people familiar with the discussions.

Outstanding issues also include ironing out differences over EU's carbon pricing tool on imported goods, its deforestation and pesticides rules.

Canada, unlike the UK, has been granted access to SAFE, the bloc's €150 billion ($173 billion) loan program for defense procurement.

Canada and the EU will be expected to make progress ahead of their summit in Montreal in October, at which they could sign a digital trade agreement that it's been in the works, said the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

"Europe and Canada believe in democracy," von der Leyen will say. "That power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest."

articles.title: We spent decades preparing for another 9/11. Another attack may look totally different
articles.summary: The United States faces a growing GPS vulnerability as adversaries develop spoofing and jamming capabilities that could cost $1 billion per day.
articles.body: The attacks of September 11 fundamentally changed how the United States thinks about national security. Over the past 25 years, we've invested enormous resources in aviation security, intelligence and counterterrorism to ensure it never happens again. But threats evolve. We don't get to choose how our adversaries attack us. History suggests they'll look for the vulnerabilities we've overlooked. And while we’ve bolstered our security and response capabilities, it’s very likely the next major conflict will find its way to our shores again with unconventional attacks on our homeland. AMERICA BUILT A FORTRESS AFTER 9/11. THEN THE THREAT STARTED HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT As we become more electronically interconnected and dependent, regardless of where the physical battles occur, the conflicts will extend domestically intent to cause disruption, panic, chaos and potential loss of lives. The U.S. must be prepared for the evolution of threats. Not designed to destroy buildings or critical infrastructure but instead designed to disrupt the core systems that allow the country to function. There is no need to physically destroy our economic, emergency response, transportation and agriculture systems if a single act can render them severely compromised. FOREIGN ENEMIES HAVE A SHOCKINGLY SIMPLE WAY TO TRACK US TROOPS OVERSEAS, LAWMAKERS WARN Our vulnerability is well documented because so much of modern life depends on a foundational core: knowing where things are. In fact, it is an assumption so deeply embedded in everyday life that it is almost invisible. Position underpins how trucks move across the country, how food is planted and harvested, how utilities restore power after disasters, how emergency responders reach people in need and how military forces maneuver, coordinate, and sustain operations. The world does not simply run on roads, communications, banking systems or the internet. It runs on position. GPS performs so reliably that we've built both military and civilian systems around the assumption that it will always be both available and trustworthy. That assumption is becoming harder to defend. Recent conflicts have demonstrated that GPS interference, spoofing and electronic warfare are no longer isolated events. They have become recurring features of modern conflict. So common that the Department of War has made the ability to function without position (contested logistics) one of its top priorities. According to the U.S. Space Force, China is actively developing and fielding counterspace capabilities intended to disrupt and degrade U.S. space-enabled capabilities. Those include anti-satellite weapons, electronic warfare systems and technologies designed to interfere with satellite operations. Our enemy is giving us their future playbook. Governments have publicly warned that adversaries continue expanding their ability to jam, spoof and disrupt satellite-based positioning. The methods vary, but they expose the same underlying dependency: countless systems rely on information that originates thousands of miles above the Earth. In June, researchers linked several brief, widespread GNSS interference events across Europe to transmissions from Russian satellites. They identified at least three incidents lasting up to 10 seconds. FBI WARNS BATTLEFIELD-STYLE DRONE ATTACKS COULD REACH US: 'ONLY A MATTER OF TIME' The reality is that every mile between the vehicle and space is another opportunity for an adversary to disrupt position. The vulnerability is not GPS itself. It is the assumption that vehicles — on the battlefield, on our highways or on city streets — foundationally depend on an external system to function. The very techniques used in conflict zones can, and likely will, also be used domestically and at large scale. And, unlike our warfighters, we are not prepared. During COVID, we experienced just a shadow of how quickly uncertainty surrounding essential goods affected public behavior and exposed the fragility of supply chains. A widespread disruption to positioning would not necessarily stop every vehicle or shut down every road. It would, however, introduce uncertainty into transportation, emergency response, fuel distribution, logistics and commerce at precisely the moment continuity matters most. While not physical terrorism, this economic terrorism would have profound implications for military mobility, emergency response, logistics and the broader economy. According to a National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)-commissioned study, a nationwide loss of GPS services would cost the U.S. economy an estimated $1 billion every day. That figure reflects direct economic impacts. The broader effects on emergency response, logistics, transportation and public confidence are far more difficult to quantify. At the same time, the United States is investing billions of dollars in autonomous systems, robotic logistics, AI-enabled command and control and next-generation military capabilities. Much of the public discussion focuses on what those technologies will eventually do. Far less attention has been paid to what they fundamentally require before they can do any of it. Whether a vehicle is operated by a soldier or independently, it must continuously know its position and remain capable of accomplishing its mission. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The United States should continue investing in artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, robotic logistics, and the technologies that will shape the future battlefield. But preparing for tomorrow cannot come at the expense of preparing for today. Twenty-five years after 9/11, the lesson is not simply that we must prepare for another attack. It is that we must prepare for the next kind of attack. The vulnerabilities are different, but the objective is the same. Strengthening the foundations that keep military forces, emergency responders and critical infrastructure moving should be treated as a national priority, not an afterthought. Innovation and readiness are not competing priorities. The best innovation strengthens readiness. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP As we build the next generation of military capability, we cannot afford to overlook the assumptions that make every future capability possible. The enemy gets a vote. Twenty-five years after 9/11, our responsibility is not simply to prepare for the last attack. It is to question the assumptions that could define the next one.

articles.title: Trump wants lower rates. His new Fed chairman is poised to raise them
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve finds itself in a confusing economic moment, but one thing has become clear: Interest rates are moving higher, likely starting Wednesday....
articles.body:
The Federal Reserve finds itself in a confusing economic moment, but one thing has become clear: Interest rates are moving higher, likely starting Wednesday. That's an awkward reality for Kevin Warsh, the Fed chairman handpicked by President Donald Trump to lower rates.

If the Fed hikes its key interest rate as Wall Street expects, it would effectively put him at odds with the president, who has continued to demand lower borrowing costs , even as inflation remains stubbornly above the Fed's 2% target.

Fed officials are expected to begin what could be a series of rate hikes designed to slow the US economy and put inflation back on track. The ongoing war in the Middle East has pushed up energy prices and now threatens to make inflation more persistent. If expectations bear out, the Fed's decision would mark the first rate increase since July 2023.

Wall Street expects the Fed to hike rates twice by year's end — this month and again in December. While that probably would not be enough to cause serious economic damage, the larger question is what happens if inflation doesn't come down.

So, the Fed is mulling how many rate hikes may be necessary, which raises the other question of how well American consumers and businesses can endure those higher rates, especially in the face of mounting consumer debt, weaker spending and longer spells of unemployment. Raising rates could weaken an economy that is already showing signs of strain.

"The odds of a serious Fed policy mistake are uncomfortably high and rising," Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's, wrote on social media. "If the Fed tightens to bring inflation down faster… that is hard to do without layoffs, rising unemployment, and igniting a self-reinforcing negative cycle."

It's unclear just how many rate increases are coming— or how many it would take to push the US economy over the edge.

One rate increase probably won't make much difference, but history shows that the Fed rarely hikes just once whenever it determines that inflation requires action. Some investors and economists even worry the handful of rate hikes the market expects might not be enough to curb AI-driven inflation , potentially requiring the Fed to push rates much higher.

"The Fed creates recessions, and it does so by taking the policy rate too high and/or keeping it there for too long," said Chris Galipeau, senior market strategist at Franklin Templeton Institute. "If we get to three (rate hikes) and go above that, then that's a really big risk."

articles.title: Lawmakers scramble to catch-up on AI
articles.summary: Washington is scrambling to manage the abrupt panic around AI development, but party politics, a limited legislative window and lack of consensus makes it an uphill, next-to-impossible task. In the wake of a researcher’s viral warning about the technology, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are floating numerous proposals to prevent the negative potential…
articles.body:
Washington is scrambling to manage the abrupt panic around AI development, but party politics, a limited legislative window and lack of consensus makes it an uphill, next-to-impossible task.

In the wake of a researcher’s viral warning about the technology, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are floating numerous proposals to prevent the negative potential of AI, while President Trump is doubling down on his light-touch approach to AI regulation.

With less than two months on the legislative calendar, the chance of moving last-minute AI safety bills through both chambers and getting the president’s signature are next to zero.

“Do you think we’re [Congress] capable of regulating AI? I mean, we can’t pass a budget, you think we’re going to have some great bill on AI?” Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) told The Hill on Tuesday.

“We’re not going to pass a smart AI bill in three weeks or this year,” he added, referring to the short window the Senate has in session before a monthlong recess for the midterms.

Capitol Hill has tried to grasp the technology for years, forming various coalitions and task forces to better understand its development and brainstorm policy. But the technology has moved faster than many expected and Congress’s timeline hasn’t kept up.

Dozens of bills regulating the safety elements of AI were introduced over the past 18 months, most of which remain stagnant due to clashing priorities on AI and the data centers that power them.

These policy fights were thrown back into the spotlight this week after 27-year-old AI researcher Jacob Coxon went viral by proclaiming the AI labs believe the technology “could kill humans” but still race towards superintelligence anyway.

Superintelligence is a hypothetical AI agent that outperforms all of humanity’s cognitive performance. Coxon and others believe this technology could reach the point of being able to self-improve itself, meaning humans can no longer control its development or intentions.

Democrats have seized on these concerns over the past year, while Trump and his base argue heavy regulation will impede AI firms ability to stay ahead of China.

But Coxon’s warning broke through the political divides and caught the attention of both parties on Capitol Hill, while simultaneously highlighting the massive hurdles Washington still faces.

Among the last-minute proposals is a bill from Republican Sen. John Kennedy (La.) that would require AI companies to implement a so-called “kill switch” into their models. This would be a safety measure that companies can use to pause or shut down certain models.

Kennedy will bring it to the floor via unanimous consent to try to bypass a formal roll-call vote, telling reporters there are no other options given the limited window left.

The Louisiana senator emphasized this does not put the government “in charge” of the so-called AI kill switch, but only requires companies to have the mechanism in place.

Trump “doesn’t want us to do anything to impede the development of American AI and he’s absolutely right and I agree with it,” Kennedy added on Tuesday. “But how is it going to impede the development of AI if we do something to gain the confidence of the American people in AI?”

Public sentiment around AI and the firms behind it has plummeted over the past year amid concerns around data centers, the labor workforce and its ability to supercharge bad actors. A Gallup poll released in July found public confidence in large technology companies was at a record-low, dropping from 32 percent in 2020 to 20 percent in 2026.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), the chair of the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee, said Coxon’s warnings were “highly concerning” and called for more guardrails.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), a frequent critic of Big Tech, said Congress has a job to ensure a “very small group of the richest people and the richest companies in the history of the world don’t end up controlling our entire economy, our entire regulatory system and the livelihoods of every American.”

When asked whether Congress is prepared to tackle this issue, Hawley sidestepped, stating he “welcomes the company” of last-ditch efforts to regulate the technology.

While Republicans are considering ways to manage the risks around AI, Trump fiercely defended his approach to AI in a series of posts Monday, alleging the warnings from Coxon and Anthropic are a “hoax.”

Some Republicans are sticking to that approach.

“If you’re the CEO of an AI company, you have an obligation not to kill your kids, and your grandkids, and so for them to come and say we need to regulate them, no they need to regulate themselves,” Scott said Tuesday. “We’re not going to put ourselves in a position to be behind China.”

Other lawmakers like Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) are suggesting new committees to “rein in” AI, but industry experts argue this will only further delay what already feels like a tall ask.

Tony Samp, the founding director of the Senate AI Caucus in 2019, pointed out there has been nearly a decade of AI forums, commissions and caucuses for policymakers to get “educated and up to speed.”

“Too often in this town, groups seek a perfect or comprehensive solution but that is not what is needed to meet this initial moment on AI models,” Samp, now principal and head of AI policy at DLA Piper, told The Hill.

On the other side of the country, some Silicon Valley executives are also trying to quell these concerns, either calling for a slowdown of the tech’s development or all-out dismissing the warnings as fear-mongering.

Following Coxon’s thread, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI CEO Elon Musk agreed a slowdown of the technology is needed.

Altman reiterated OpenAI’s support of a federal framework for safety requirements, but he also argued the industry does not need to wait for legislation or an antitrust exemption to create “consistent rules” and shared values among the firms.

Others like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dismissed these warnings, and without an industry or international cooperation, it is not clear whether companies will be willing to make changes. Chris LeHane, OpenAI’s global affairs chief, said Tuesday the firm still believes “the policy window is open.”

“We’re well aware there’s a limited amount of time over the calendar, certainly before the midterms actually take place,” LeHane told reporters in Washington.

If lawmakers miss the window, it is likely to face more hurdles should Democrats take control of the House or Senate under Trump.

“Given that [a] divided government is assured no matter what happens in the election, the difference between what’s achievable this year and next may not be all that great,” one technology lobbyist told The Hill Tuesday.

“If members truly feel urgency then they’ll work to pass something meaningful this year,” the lobbyist added.

Julia Shapero and Helen Huiskes contributed.

articles.title: Massie says he hid Hegseth impeachment resolution from GOP leaders
articles.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) said Tuesday he kept his resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth a secret from Republican leaders because he did not want to “show his hand.” The Kentucky Republican, who has been a frequent critic of the Trump administration’s military operations in Iran, introduced his resolution on the House floor Tuesday…
articles.body:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) said Tuesday he kept his resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth a secret from Republican leaders because he did not want to “show his hand.”

The Kentucky Republican, who has been a frequent critic of the Trump administration’s military operations in Iran, introduced his resolution on the House floor Tuesday afternoon.

“I didn’t want to show it to anybody,” he said during an appearance on CNN’s “The Source” later that evening. “I was afraid that they would do something to subvert me getting on the floor for an hour and 20 minutes and reading these articles.”

Massie told host Kaitlan Collins that he had “not heard” back from House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) about his resolution, noting the GOP leader has “48 hours” to call a vote.

“This is a hot war,” he said. “This could become a nuclear war, and in the interim, even if it doesn’t, there are civilian casualties that are racking up greater than they would have otherwise because another one of my articles of impeachment shows that Peter Hegseth has degraded the ability of the DOD to minimize civilian casualties.”

It is unclear whether any other Republicans will join him in the effort to impeach Hegseth.

Massie previously introduced resolutions to limit President Trump’s military operations in Iran. The House has passed three war powers resolutions with the support of several Republicans, with the most recent one advancing Tuesday.

The lawmaker lost his primary reelection bid to Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein (R) in the Bluegrass State’s May primary. Hegseth traveled to Kentucky ahead of the GOP race to campaign for Gallrein, a former Navy SEAL.

Attorney General Todd Blanche also defended Hegseth on Tuesday when asked by a reporter during a Rose Garden press briefing about Massie’s impeachment resolution.

“Secretary Hegseth is doing a phenomenal job, and the secretary of war doesn’t just go off and do things,” Blanche said. “He follows the law, and so the [Justice Department] plays a role in that and we play an active role in making sure the law’s complied with.”

In a statement Tuesday, Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson called Hegseth a “transformative leader.”

“By every measurable metric, the Department of War is better under President Trump and Secretary Hegseth’s leadership than before,” Wilson said. “The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first.”
