articles.title: A brief history of AI executives calling for regulation
articles.summary: Here are the times when OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and Elon Musk warned about the dangers of AI, ahead of their recent public agreement to slow their roll.
articles.body: Over the past few days, a lot of people who stand to make a lot of money from AI all publicly agreed that it’s time to make everyone slow down before we lose control — including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, and X CEO Elon Musk. When people who profit from something declare that it’s dangerous and needs to be regulated, there’s always reason to be skeptical. But whatever their reason, this is far from the first time AI thought leaders have sounded the alarm. Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution prompted author Samuel Butler to warn about intelligent self-replicating machines replacing humans back in 1863 — and in his follow-up 1872 book Erewhon, he describes visiting a fictional society that has already regulated machines out of existence to avoid humanity’s collapse. Computing pioneer Alan Turing famously warned in a 1951 lecture that artificial intelligence would “meet with great opposition,” because undying machines “would not take long to outstrip our feeble powers” and would eventually “take control.” Calls for intervention, too, aren’t new. In 2000, Sun Microsystems cofounder and chief scientist Bill Joy wrote that self-replicating robots could be more dangerous than nuclear weapons, partly because they’re being developed “within the now-unchallenged system of global capitalism” rather than in tightly controlled government labs. And in 2009, Microsoft researcher Eric Horvitz, who now serves as the company’s chief scientific officer, brought leading AI researchers together to consider “creating policies that might constrain or bias the behaviors of autonomous and semi-autonomous systems so as to address concerns.” But modern AI bigwigs warning that their investments should be controlled? That trend appears to have begun with Elon Musk, who invested earlier than most. July 2017: Elon Musk says we need to regulate AI before it becomes a danger to humanity By the time Elon Musk told a gathering of US governors that they needed to regulate AI right away, the SpaceX and Tesla CEO already had skin in the game. He’d already invested $38 million in OpenAI, as well as stakes in at least two other AI companies, and he’d publicly spoken about the dangers of AI for three years. In June 2014, he suggested AI research could produce a real-life Terminator, called AI “potentially more dangerous than nukes” that August, and suggested that working on AI was “summoning the demon” that October. In January 2015, he joined Stephen Hawking in signing an open letter asking for responsible AI research; Hawking had previously warned that the creation of AI might be the last thing humans ever do. “AI is a rare case where we need to be proactive about regulation instead of reactive. Because I think by the time we are reactive in AI regulation, it’s too late,” Musk told a gathering of US governors at the July 2017 National Governors Association summer meeting. In March 2018, he added: “AI is far more dangerous than nukes. So why do we have no regulatory oversight?” March 2018: Mark Zuckerberg is ‘actually not sure we shouldn’t be regulated’ In the wake of Facebook’s Cambridge Analytica data scandal, the Meta founder suggested his company should be regulated — if it’s the “right” regulation. It was largely not about AI, but he did go there: > Now that companies increasingly over the next five to 10 years, as AI tools get better and better, will be able to proactively determine what might be offensive content or violate some rules, what therefore is the responsibility and legal responsibility of companies to do that? In March 2019, he added that the internet needs a “more active role” for regulators. December 2018: Microsoft sounds an alarm over facial recognition technology Earlier in 2018, Microsoft began taking fire for working with ICE on facial recognition technologies, at a time many tech CEOs had condemned Donald Trump’s policy of separating children from parents who are arrested at the US border. While this form of AI isn’t quite the same as self-replicating intelligence, Microsoft president Brad Smith opened the door to voluntary regulation in a speech at the Brookings Institution, saying, “We believe it’s important for governments in 2019 to start adopting laws to regulate this technology. … We believe that the only way to protect against this race to the bottom is to build a floor of responsibility that supports healthy market competition. And a solid floor requires that we ensure that this technology, and the organizations that develop and use it, are governed by the rule of law.” January 2020: Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai says there is ‘no question’ that AI needs to be regulated “[T]here is no question in my mind that artificial intelligence needs to be regulated. It is too important not to,” wrote Pichai in an editorial for the Financial Times. “The only question is how to approach it.” “Companies such as ours cannot just build promising new technology and let market forces decide how it will be used,” he added. Like with Microsoft a year earlier, these comments emerged around fears about AI facial recognition specifically. March 2023: Elon Musk and top AI researchers call for pause on ‘giant AI experiments’ In 2023, as generative AI fervor began to reshape the entire tech industry, scientists began suggesting that companies should slow down their research — or else. “If such a pause cannot be enacted quickly, governments should step in and institute a moratorium,” the letter, published by the nonprofit Future of Life Institute and signed by Musk, among others, reads. Two weeks later, Musk announced he’d created his own new AI company. Two years later, he would use DOGE to dismantle chunks of the federal workforce instead of helping to regulate anything. May 16th, 2023: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman asks Congress to regulate AI Brought before the US Senate for a series of AI hearings, Altman agreed that Congress should create a new agency to regulate artificial intelligence. “We believe that the benefits of the tools we have deployed so far vastly outweigh the risks,” he argued. “However, we think that regulatory intervention by governments will be critical to mitigate the risks of increasingly powerful models.” In another hearing on May 25th, Anthropic’s CEO warned US senators that AI could help create bioweapons. May 25th, 2023: Microsoft president Brad Smith ‘details five ways governments should consider policies, laws, and regulations around AI’ When OpenAI’s CEO was before Congress, we noted that the tone was friendly and they seemed to be trying to shape legislation together; here is an example of Microsoft trying to shape future regulation as well. One regulatory example: “New laws would require operators of these systems to build safety brakes into high-risk AI systems by design. The government would then ensure that operators test high-risk systems regularly to make certain that the system safety measures are effective.” May 30th, 2023: Top AI researchers and CEOs warn against ‘risk of extinction’ in 22-word statement “Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.” While the 22-word statement doesn’t explicitly ask the government to step in, it’s hard to think world leaders wouldn’t raise their eyebrows even higher than before. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and then-Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis were among the cosigners. September 2023: Mark Zuckerberg wants everyone to ‘work together’ on regulation In a private Senate meeting, closed to the public and media, tech CEOs reportedly agreed that the AI industry needed regulation. One set of remarks was not so private: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said that “Congress should engage with AI to support innovation and safeguards.” “We think policymakers, academics, civil society, and industry should all work together to minimize the potential risks of this new technology, but also to maximize the potential benefits.” Between July 2023 and May 2024, tech companies signed a flurry of nonbinding agreements with governments that would supposedly keep them in check: * July 2023: Meta, Google, and OpenAI promise the White House they’ll develop AI responsibly * September 2023: More companies commit to the White House AI safety accord * November 2023: At UK’s AI Summit developers and govts agree on testing to help manage risks * May 2024: AI Seoul Summit: World leaders agree to launch network of safety institutes Also in September 2023: A book from Inflection AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman — who is now Microsoft’s AI chief — argued that governments should regulate. August–September 2024: Elon Musk and Anthropic come out in favor of California’s AI safety bill “This is a tough call and will make some people upset, but, all things considered, I think California should probably pass the SB 1047 AI safety bill,” Musk posted in August. Anthropic originally came out against it in July, as did OpenAI in August, but Anthropic changed its tune in September. California Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed SB 1047, though, stating that “I do not believe this is the best approach to protecting the public from real threats posed by the technology.” October 2024: Anthropic calls for ‘targeted regulation’ “Governments should urgently take action on AI policy in the next eighteen months. The window for proactive risk prevention is closing fast,” Anthropic wrote in an open letter (bolding theirs). “It is critical over the next year that policymakers, the AI industry, safety advocates, civil society, and lawmakers work together to develop an effective regulatory framework,” the company added. January 2025: OpenAI submits its ‘policy proposals’ The document begins by suggesting the UK stunted the development of its own automobile industry with regulation, while proposing “democratic AI” instead: “Rules and regulations for the development and use of AI should be based on the democratic values the country has always stood for.” June 2025: Anthropic CEO: Don’t let AI companies off the hook In a guest essay for The New York Times, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote: “Federal law does not compel us or any other A.I. company to be transparent about our models’ capabilities or to take any meaningful steps toward risk reduction. Some companies can simply choose not to.” The essay is against the Trump administration’s proposed 10-year moratorium on US states regulating AI. He wasn’t arguing for a slowdown, though, but rather a “national transparency standard” that “would help not only the public but also Congress understand how the technology is developing.” September 2025: Anthropic endorses California’s SB 53 As California tried to regulate its AI giants again, Anthropic threw its support in early, and this one actually became law. It’s a transparency standard, like the one Anthropic was asking for, with safety reporting requirements and whistleblower protection. OpenAI lobbied against it. September 2026: The AI industry seemingly agrees to slow down — while Trump calls AI fears ‘a sick conspiracy’ This summer, shit hit the fan. It became public that rogue AI agents can — and did — attack other companies. OpenAI said it hit the brakes in August, and on September 8th, a senior Anthropic safety researcher resigned in protest, declaring there’s a 10 percent chance AI could kill all humans by the end of the decade. Another Anthropic safety researcher agreed. Now, suddenly, the AI industry has seemingly agreed to slow down the pace of development. More: * Anthropic CEO says it’s time to pump the brakes on AI * Microsoft says ‘people matter more than AI’ following safety concerns * What execs and politicians are saying about slowing down AI development * Is Big Tech’s AI slowdown a safety pact or a cartel? Is this a new call for regulation? From Anthropic’s CEO, it seems to be. In his essay “We Must Pace the Frontier,” Amodei writes that “The most effective method of pacing is via regulation that targets all US frontier AI companies, as that covers even those who are unwilling to cooperate voluntarily,” and he suggests governments might embed people inside AI companies to help prevent incidents. It’s not clear every AI company wants to go that far. “Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman writes. But Altman does say that he’ll commit to “independent evaluators with employee-like access” as well. Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg also doesn’t seem to be aligned. On September 15th, he posted that each company has its own individual responsibility to move at the right pace and that Meta is already doing so. He also prominently linked back to his manifesto from August, which contains this line: “Any policy that slows American model releases -- even by a month -- could add significant risk to American leadership while letting foreign models race ahead.” Regardless of what tech leaders are saying, regulation seems highly unlikely to come under the Trump administration, which has signaled it wants the industry barreling full speed ahead. Even if these companies don’t actually want the regulation they seem to be asking for, this is one of the loudest alarm bells they’ve sounded so far — and the world is watching.

articles.title: Bond market woes likely a factor for Fed, but intervention seen as unlikely
articles.summary: By Michael S.
articles.body:
Sept 16 (Reuters) - Surging government bond yields are raising credit costs across the U.S. economy and could factor into Federal Reserve monetary policy deliberations, but analysts see the central bank resisting any explicit call from the Trump administration to bail out the market.

The focus on the Fed's possible involvement comes as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has taken an ‌unusually activist role in trying to tamp down rising yields he considers to be misaligned with the U.S. economic outlook.

Bessent's campaign, which saw the expansion of a key debt buyback operation last week, ‌is foundering, as the 10-year Treasury note rose above 5% to its highest since 2007. He shrugged the move off as owing to "global issues" on Tuesday as he arrived for a congressional hearing.

Treasury's bond market travails are raising questions whether the Fed might be requested ​to buy government debt to reduce supply, which could cap or lower yields, in turn easing government and private sector borrowing costs.

Fed watchers see little prospect for that outside of markets tumbling into distress, though there's little evidence of that so far even with the steady slide in prices. That said, the question has persisted given comments by Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh that have signaled a greater willingness to coordinate with Treasury on some issues.

"One of the Fed's unwritten mandates is financial conditions," said Rick Rieder, BlackRock Inc's chief bond investment manager, who was under consideration by Trump to be Fed leader. Noting that Fed policymakers influence the cost of debt through their adjustments to short-term interest rates, he ‌said that "has to be part of the criteria they consider" in any monetary ⁠policy decisions.

The Fed on Wednesday is expected to wrap up its two-day meeting with policymakers raising their policy rate by a quarter percentage point to 3.75% to 4.00% because recent inflation readings have been too high. Market participants believe this could help Treasury's cause because it will bolster the Fed's inflation-fighting credibility, which should help longer-dated yields ⁠come down over time.

A Deutsche Bank poll of investors released Monday found that investors see a rate hike now as likely lifting yields slightly over the short term, but they see long-term yields going up even more if the Fed were to leave rates steady.

If the Treasury encounters significant headwinds selling its debt or there were other market dislocations, the Fed could be drawn in more to buy debt to calm conditions, Rieder said. That makes it important to watch how coming debt ​auctions ​perform.

articles.title: ‘You can’t trust anything’ from Anthropic, OpenAI leaders, lawyer says
articles.summary: Attorney Jay Edelson slammed the heads of the leading artificial intelligence companies Tuesday, declaring “you can’t trust anything” they say. Appearing on News Nation with Leland Vittert, Edelson – who is currently leading lawsuits against OpenAI, Anthropic and other major technology companies – was asked if he had ever seen leaders within an industry abdicate…
articles.body:
Attorney Jay Edelson slammed the heads of the leading artificial intelligence companies Tuesday, declaring “you can’t trust anything” they say.

Appearing on News Nation with Leland Vittert, Edelson – who is currently leading lawsuits against OpenAI, Anthropic and other major technology companies – was asked if he had ever seen leaders within an industry abdicate “any responsibility to make their products any safer” while “arguing that their products are insanely dangerous.”

“I don’t think we should lump everyone in together, but I agree. You can’t trust anything that comes out of Dario’s mouth or Sam Altman’s mouth,” Edelson said.

He continued that not all tech leaders are following those patterns, citing xAI CEO Elon Musk’s lawsuit against OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman which attempted to force the company to become a nonprofit again and “put safety first.”

“They’re doing it because they think they can make more money in the long run. Now if they’re saying, yeah, we admit it, we have no control over our systems, which is partially true, but not fully true,” he said.

His remarks come after several current and former Anthropic and OpenAI researchers warned that both companies are acting irresponsibly as they race toward superintelligence and accused the AI firms of “ gambling with our lives .”

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic and OpenAI, wrote in a post on the social platform X .

Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, affirmed Coxon’s warning, stating, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”

When asked why leadership at these firms were not scared of its technology doing harm , Edelson described a six-sided dice where one side would cause this mass extinction event Coxon warned about.

“And Sam doesn’t care. He’s willing to roll that dice,” he said. “But I think most normal people, if they really thought they were putting out a product that could have an extinction level event, they would actually pull the product from market. And that’s not what any of them are saying.”

“They’re just saying, maybe we should think a little bit about it,” he stated.

After the researchers’ warnings, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Altman and Musk made similar calls to slow down AI capability development. “And Sam doesn’t care. He’s willing to roll that dice,” he said. “But I think most normal people, if they really thought they were putting out a product that could have an extinction level event, they would actually pull the product from market. And that’s not what any of them are saying.”

After the researchers’ warnings, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI CEO Elon Musk made similar calls to slow down AI capability development.

The Pentagon is reportedly requiring troops to meet waist-to-height requirements and exhibit “impeccable” grooming standards in order to attend Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s “State of the Force” address later this month.

The Wall Street Journal published a report Tuesday which included emails from the Pentagon to Army commanders stating that troops must have “impeccable grooming and uniform standards (no exception)” to attend the State of the Force address.

The emails said members selected to attend must be “consistently rated as top performers within their formations”; have a “clear record of integrity, discipline and selfless service”; “demonstrate strong presence, clear communication and sound judgment under pressure”; and “serve as role models for their peers and subordinates,” per the Journal.

The standards were reportedly sent to commanders throughout the military outlining who can be selected as audience members for the address. Candidates can include lower-ranking officials and enlisted service members.

Those who are selected to attend the event will also have the opportunity to work out with the Defense secretary based on “demonstrated leadership quality and professional character,” according to the Journal.

The Pentagon’s email comes almost a year after it unveiled new grooming standards , specifically new criteria pertaining to facial hair.

“The grooming standard set by the U.S. military is to be clean shaven and neat in presentation for a proper military appearance,” Hegseth said when the standards were announced.

Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesperson, said service members would be able to obtain shaving waivers through military medical officials but ultimately the commander was the final approving authority.

Hegseth has also enforced screening policies for male active-duty and reserve service members who are older than 30, checking testosterone levels with blood tests and offering testosterone replacement therapy as a treatment.

Female service members are asked whether they have disrupted menstrual cycles that could be linked with hormonal dysregulation, according to the guidelines.

“This initiative, it’s not about artificial enhancement; it’s about restoring and optimizing your natural capabilities, protecting your longevity, ensuring you have the biological foundation required to sustain and fight,” Hegseth stated in a video announcement two months ago.

The Pentagon did not respond to The Hill’s request for immediate comment.

articles.body:
Vice President Vance weighed in on the ongoing AI safety debate Tuesday, pressing those behind the technology to be careful.

“The president, I think, is very rightly asking the question, why is it that the people who are at the frontier of the AI economy are throwing up their hands and saying, ‘Well, we’ve built Frankenstein,’ and the solution to Frankenstein, apparently, is to create a one-world governance structure for artificial intelligence?” Vance said Tuesday during an event for the “All-In Podcast.”

“What I would say to those people — if you’re building Frankenstein, stop, or maybe build, you know, if the cat is out of the bag, then build the defensive mechanism against Frankenstein,” he added.

President Trump on Monday defended his approach to AI , stating that the only protections required are a strong president amid calls for safety guardrails around the technology.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “The Trump Administration has stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things.’”

Over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said that AI development must be slowed to give space for the implementation of necessary risk prevention safeguards, with fellow tech moguls Sam Altman and Elon Musk backing him up.

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in a blog post. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”

The Anthropic CEO recommended that AI companies quickly undertake measures aimed at “pacing” the development of models and warned of potentially grim consequences if the technology does not have brakes.

articles.body:
Rep. Joe Wilson (R-S.C.) is demanding the NHL investigate Washington Capitals star Alex Ovechkin over an advertisement he participated in promoting Russian President Vladimir Putin’s party ahead of the country’s elections this weekend.

In a letter to NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman on Wednesday, Wilson called it “incredibly alarming” that Ovechkin appeared in the ad “supporting the party of war criminal Putin.”

“American hockey fans deserve better leadership from their star players,” the Republican wrote.

Ovechkin appeared in the ad along with a number of other famous Russian athletes, celebrities and politicians under the tagline “when we are united, we are invincible.”

The advertisement has sparked widespread backlash given Putin’s long documented history of crimes against humanity and his ongoing war with Ukraine.

The NHL’s all time leading goal scorer has not weighed in publicly on the ad, but, in a statement to The Athletic this week, the Capitals attempted to distance the club from the incident.

“Alex Ovechkin is a Russian citizen who lives in Moscow with his family during the offseason and will live there following his retirement,” a team spokesperson told the outlet. “This summer, while in Russia, he was asked by his country to participate in a video campaign. As the longest-tenured athlete in Washington, D.C. and a pillar of the community, his focus and ours is on the season ahead and the continued impact he makes on the ice and in our city.”

Wilson is among the most prominent critics of Russia on Capitol Hill and insisted that Bettman clarify the NHL’s policies on its players appearing in political advertisements “on behalf of doctorial political parties and foreign political regimes.”

“The NHL and the Washington Capitals have an extraordinary platform and responsibility,” the South Carolina lawmaker wrote. “I hope the league will treat this matter with the seriousness it deserves and I look forward to your response.”

articles.title: Hackers rip down Flock camera, steal its data, share findings with media
articles.summary: A group of hackers ripped down a Flock camera and stole its data, finding that the cameras’ software can generate dozens of images from a single passing vehicle to develop its signature. The group, called stegan0gram, shared findings with Wired and 404 Media, who ran a joint investigation. The outlets found that in a 21-day…
articles.body:
A group of hackers ripped down a Flock camera and stole its data, finding that the cameras’ software can generate dozens of images from a single passing vehicle to develop its signature.

The group, called stegan0gram, shared findings with Wired and 404 Media , who ran a joint investigation. The outlets found that in a 21-day period the camera photographed roughly 50,200 vehicles and generated about 1.6 million images.

Flock has a system of license plate readers, video cameras and audio detection devices incorporated into its AI database. That database logs license plate numbers, as well as car features like make, model, color and bumper stickers. Local jurisdictions can share data with other law enforcement agencies, creating a major network that law enforcement can use in crime solving.

The outlets stated that the camera generally captures around 28 images from a single encounter with a vehicle, though some can produce more than 100, and sends photos and other data to Flock through a cellular network. They noted that the camera does not identify vehicles or read plates, stating that this analysis appears to happen on Flock’s servers.

In one instance, the camera — which runs about 20 Flock-built apps including apps that detect motion and upload data — was able to detect an American flag patch located on a motorcyclist’s saddle bag, per 404 Media and Wired.

One hacker affiliated with stegan0gram told the outlets, “We liberated hardware in the field, disarmed them, and proceeded with reverse engineering of the cameras and associated solar equipment.”

“Why just destroy them when we can reverse engineer them and find the secrets of those spying on us?” they added.

When asked about the investigation, a spokesperson from Flock told The Hill, “The unauthorized removal and tampering of a Flock camera is illegal.”

“Flock takes security seriously and maintains a public Vulnerability Disclosure Policy for security researchers to report potential vulnerabilities directly to us,” the spokesperson said. “We received no report through that process, and based on the limited information provided, we do not have enough detail to assess the claims being made.”

The surveillance technology has become controversial among lawmakers, with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) saying earlier this month that he worried the Sunshine State would become a “digital AI surveillance state where everything we’re doing is being tracked at all times.”

Rep Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) also unveiled a bill this month that aims at restricting the use of federal funds for automated license plate reader cameras and biometric surveillance cameras. It is called the Flock-Off Act.

President Trump stated his support for the technology Sunday.

“No, I sort of like them [Flock cameras] because of that, because of law enforcement. But some people don’t. They think it’s an infringement,” the president said, adding later, “I like them.”

articles.title: Zuckerberg: AI companies incentivized toward safety

articles.body:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg on Tuesday argued that artificial intelligence (AI) companies are incentivized toward safety when it comes to the timing of crafting their models and that external pressure is not needed to keep to that timeline.

“Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens,” the tech mogul wrote in a post on the social platform X.

Zuckerberg also asserted in his Tuesday post that “people won’t want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don’t do what they ask,” putting pressure on AI creators to align models more with human values.

“There is a lot of debate about slowing progress on capabilities until alignment catches up,” he added. “My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn’t focus on alignment will fall behind.”

Zuckerberg’s post follows a larger debate in the past week over AI development, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei saying over the weekend that development of the technology must be slowed to give space for the implementation of necessary risk prevention safeguards. Fellow tech moguls Sam Altman and Elon Musk backed Amodei up.

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in a blog post. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”

The Anthropic CEO recommended that AI companies quickly undertake measures aimed at “pacing” the development of models and warned of potentially grim consequences if the technology does not have brakes.
